name: The Loaded Question
statement: A question is phrased so that any direct answer concedes a controversial, unproven assumption.
statementAccent: any direct answer concedes a controversial, unproven assumption
meaning: A loaded question is a form of complex question that embeds a controversial or unproven assumption, so that any direct "yes" or "no" answer forces the respondent to implicitly accept it. The classic illustration is "Have you stopped beating your wife?" — either answer implies past beating. Whether a question is loaded depends on context: the same question can be fair in one setting and fallacious in another.
mechanism: The question is really a compressed pair — "Did you ever beat your wife?" and "If so, have you stopped?" — bundled so that only the second can be answered, forcing tacit agreement with the first. It exploits the normal expectation that a question can be answered directly, denying the respondent the chance to reject the hidden premise before answering.

examples.text: "Have you stopped beating your wife?" is the traditional example: "yes" implies past beating now ceased, "no" implies beating that continues — both concede the premise.
Diogenes Laërtius records a philosopher asked whether he had stopped beating his father, who refused the binary trap by replying "I have not beaten him, and I have not left off."
"Who is the King of France?" is an illegitimate complex question, since it falsely presumes France currently has a monarchy at all.

whyItMatters: Loaded questions are used in courtrooms, journalism, debates, and surveys to manipulate answers or trap respondents into implicit admissions, so recognising and defusing them — by challenging the embedded assumption rather than answering directly — is a core critical-thinking and cross-examination skill.
limits: A question with a presupposition is not automatically fallacious — "Who is the monarch of the United Kingdom?" presupposes a widely accepted fact and is legitimate. The wife-beating question stops being loaded where the beating has already been established, such as a trial after admission.
misreadings: It is often confused with begging the question; both smuggle in an assumption, but a loaded question specifically constrains the space of acceptable direct answers, while begging the question is a circular argument structure.
origin: The pattern was recognised by Aristotle, who classified "the making of more than one question into one" among his fallacies; the Latin designation for the general form is plurium interrogationum ("of many questions").
